title: Native pronunciation
theme: Word stress, sentence stress (content vs function words), weak forms (schwa), connected speech (linking, intrusive sounds, assimilation, elision), contractions, intonation
goal: Student speaks with native-like rhythm and stress — knowing which words to stress, which to weaken, and how to link sounds across word boundaries.
connects_to: M21 (Fala como nativo) — moves from sound shape to lexical and pragmatic native-like choices.
module_chunks: content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs) = stressed
function words (articles, prepositions, auxiliaries, pronouns) = weak/unstressed
weak forms with schwa: of /əv/, for /fə/, to /tə/, and /ən/, a /ə/, the /ðə/, you /jə/
contractions: he's, she's, we'd, they've, won't, can't, shouldn't, wouldn't
intonation: yes/no rise, wh-fall, statement fall, list rise-rise-fall

units.title: Word stress
units.grammar_focus: Word stress in multi-syllable words — especially noun/verb pairs (PROduce/proDUCE, CONtract/conTRACT) and Latinate words (phoTOgraphy, photoGRAphic)
units.real_life_context: You stress the right syllable so listeners parse the word without effort — wrong stress is one of the biggest comprehension blockers in C1+ speech.

grammar.explanation: "PHO-tograph" — stress on first syllable. Compare with "phoTOgraphy" (stress on second) and "photoGRAphic" (stress on third). The same root shifts stress based on the suffix. C2 mastery includes knowing how word formation shifts stress.

grammar.sentence: "I bought a record": where is the stress in "record"?
grammar.explanation: As a thing (a record), the stress goes at the start: REcord. As an action (to record), it moves to the end: "I want to reCORD it". Same with PREsent / preSENT and PERmit / perMIT.

"COMfortable" — stress on the first syllable. In fast speech natives often say it in three syllables ("COMF-ter-ble"). Many learners stress "comFORtable", which sounds foreign. Long words like this often keep the stress at the start.

"deVELop" — stress on second syllable. Pattern for similar verbs: deCIDE, reMEMber, beGIN, dis-COVer, sup-PORT. Two-or-three-syllable verbs often stress the second syllable (especially with prefixes de-, re-, dis-). Wrong stress in everyday verbs is a major C2 fluency leak.

grammar.passage: A: What's in the box? B: A present for you. I want to present it at dinner tonight, in front of everyone.
grammar.question: What does B want to do at dinner?
grammar.answer: give A the present in front of everyone
grammar.explanation: "A PREsent" is the gift; "to preSENT" is to give it formally. Same letters, different stress, different meaning.

listening_speaking.text: Take a PHO-tograph, study the phoTO-graphy, become photo-GRAphic.
REcord a podcast — but first, reCORD the file path.
This is a COMfortable chair — entirely COMfortable.
They deVELop software but DEvelopment takes time.
The PROduce was fresh; the team will proDUCE another batch.

units.title: Sentence stress and weak forms
units.grammar_focus: Content words (stressed) vs function words (weak/unstressed), schwa /ə/ in weak forms (of, for, to, and, a, the)
units.real_life_context: You speak with the rhythm of English — stressing meaning-carrying words and weakening grammar-glue words.

grammar.sentence: "I want a cup of tea": which words are stressed?
grammar.explanation: Content words (nouns: cup, tea; verbs: want; sometimes pronouns: I) carry stress. Function words (a, of, the, am, is) weaken. In normal speech: "I WANT a CUP of TEA" with "a" and "of" reduced to schwa /ə/. Stress = meaning markers.
grammar.listen: I want a cup of tea.

grammar.sentence: "A cup of tea": how does "of" sound?
grammar.explanation: Function words like "of", "to", "a" and "for" lose their full vowel in connected speech and become short and weak. Only the content words (cup, tea) keep full stress. Saying "of" clearly every time is one of the strongest markers of a non-native rhythm.

grammar.sentence: "I want to go": how does "to" sound?
grammar.explanation: In connected speech "to" is unstressed and its vowel reduces to a short, neutral sound: "I want tuh go". In very fast casual speech it merges further into "wanna". The full "two" is only used for emphasis or at the end of a sentence ("Where do you want to?").

options: I AM going TO the STORE
I AM GOING TO THE STORE
grammar.explanation: Equal stress on every word ("I AM going TO the STORE") sounds robotic. Native rhythm contracts ("I'm / I am") and weakens function words ("going tə the"). Only content words get full stress: "I'm / I am GOing to the STORE". Stress-timed rhythm.

grammar.passage: A: Do you want to grab a coffee before the meeting? B: I'd love to, but I've got to finish this report first.
grammar.question: Why can't B get a coffee now?
grammar.answer: B has to finish a report first
grammar.explanation: In fast speech "I've got to" sounds almost like "I've gotta", and "want to" like "wanna". The stressed words carry the meaning: COFfee, MEETing, FInish, REport.

listening_speaking.text: I WANT a CUP of TEA.

units.title: Connected speech
units.real_life_context: You connect sounds across word boundaries — the way fluent English actually runs together.

grammar.explanation: Linking: when a word ends in a consonant and the next begins with a vowel, the consonant attaches to the next word in connected speech. "An apple" → "a-NAP-pl". "Stop it" → "sto-PIT". "Find out" → "fine-DOUT". Native rhythm relies on this linking.

options: Like three separate words, with pauses
grammar.explanation: Natives link the words: "pi-ki-tup". A word ending in a consonant joins the next word starting with a vowel. Same with "turn it off" ("tur-ni-toff") and "an apple" ("a-napple").

options: What do you want to do?
What did you want to do?
Where do you want to go?
grammar.answer: What do you want to do?
grammar.explanation: In fast casual speech "what do you" becomes "whaddaya" and "want to" becomes "wanna". You will hear this all the time in films and conversations.

options: I don't know, I've got to go.
I didn't know, I got to go.
grammar.answer: I don't know, I've got to go.
grammar.explanation: "Dunno" = I don't know; "gotta" = (I've) got to. Natives drop and merge sounds when they speak fast.

grammar.passage: A: Whaddaya wanna do tonight? B: Dunno. Gonna stay in, I guess. I'm kinda tired.
grammar.question: What is B probably going to do tonight?
grammar.explanation: "Whaddaya wanna" = what do you want to; "dunno" = I don't know; "gonna" = going to; "kinda" = kind of. This is how the sentences really sound in casual speech.

units.title: Intonation
units.grammar_focus: Intonation patterns — yes/no question rise, wh-question fall, statement fall, list rise-rise-fall, sarcasm/disbelief patterns
units.real_life_context: You signal meaning through pitch — questions, statements, lists, emotional nuance.

grammar.sentence: "Are you ready?": what does the voice do at the end?
grammar.explanation: Yes/no questions typically end with rising intonation. "Are you ready?" rises on "ready". Compare with wh-questions ("What time is it?") which fall on the last content word. Rising intonation signals expectation of yes/no answer.

grammar.sentence: "What time is it?": what does the voice do at the end?
grammar.explanation: Wh-questions typically fall at the end. "What time is it?" — falling pitch on "is it". The question word itself signals that a specific answer is expected, so the rising pattern of yes/no questions isn't needed.

grammar.sentence: What does the voice do on the last item of the list?
grammar.explanation: In a list, the voice goes up on each item ("eggs, milk, bread") and comes down on the last one ("and butter") to show the list is finished. If it stays up, the listener waits for more.
grammar.listen: I need eggs, milk, bread and butter.

grammar.explanation: The words are a statement ("You're coming tonight"), but the voice goes up at the end, so it's a question. In casual English, intonation alone can turn a statement into a question.

grammar.passage: A: I just finished my first marathon! B: You finished a marathon? That's amazing!
grammar.question: How does B feel?
grammar.explanation: B repeats the news with the voice going up ("You finished a marathon?") to show surprise, then confirms with "That's amazing!".

units.title: Contractions and elision
units.grammar_focus: Contractions (he's, we'd, won't, shouldn't, mightn't) and elision (drop of /t/ /d/ between consonants — "next month" → "nex' month")
units.real_life_context: You produce the contractions and droppings that fluent English flows on — never speaking entirely "carefully" in conversation.

grammar.explanation: "He's / He is going" — contraction of "he is". The apostrophe replaces the missing letter. C2 speakers default to contractions in spoken English. Writing without contractions reads as formal or stiff; speaking without contractions reads as foreign.

"Shouldn't / Should not have" — standard written contraction of "should not have". In casual fast speech, often produced as "shouldn'ta" /ˈʃʊdn(ə)tə/ — the "have" reduces to a schwa-only sound. C2 listeners parse this; speakers may produce it in casual register.

options: I'm going to call you later.
grammar.answer: I'm going to call you later.
grammar.explanation: "Gonna" = going to; "ya" = you. This is how the sentence really sounds in casual speech.

options: I would of gone if I would know.
I have gone if I knew.
grammar.explanation: "I would have gone if I had known" → casual contracted: "I'd / I would've gone if I'd known". Two contractions stacked: "I'd / I would" (I would) and "'ve" (have). In writing, "I would've" is common; "I'd / I would've" is very informal and mostly spoken. C2 listeners recognise these even when they don't appear in print.

grammar.passage: A: You shouldn't've told him. B: I know. I'll call him next month and say sorry.
grammar.question: When will B call him?
grammar.explanation: "Shouldn't've" = should not have, said fast; "next month" sounds like "nex' month". Natives drop sounds like this all the time.

listening_speaking.text: He's been here for two hours.
We'd've left earlier if we could.

cross_unit_consolidation: Stress the correct syllable in multi-syllable words (PHO-tograph vs pho-TO-graphy vs photo-GRAphic)
Distinguish noun-verb pairs by stress (PROduce/proDUCE, REcord/reCORD)
Stress content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs) and weaken function words (articles, prepositions, auxiliaries) — the stress-timed rhythm of English
Produce weak forms with schwa /ə/ for "of", "to", "and", "a", "the"
Link consonant + vowel across word boundaries ("an apple" → "a-napple")
Apply assimilation in casual fast speech ("don't you" → "doncha", "did you" → "didja")
Elide /t/ /d/ in consonant clusters ("next month" → "nex' month")
Choose intonation patterns for function (rising yes/no question, falling wh-question, list rise-rise-rise-fall, falling-flat for sarcasm)
Use contractions and stacked contractions naturally ("he's", "we'd've", "shouldn'ta")
